title: Disaster recovery planning
description: Build a disaster recovery plan for Azure workloads using backup, Azure Site Recovery, and multi-region patterns. Learn recovery strategies, test your failover, and document runbooks.

data.text: Disaster recovery is the process of restoring service after a major incident—whether that incident is a fire in the datacenter, a region-wide outage, or a ransomware attack. A disaster recovery plan defines what to back up, where to replicate it, how to restore it, and who is responsible for each step.

Azure supports four common recovery strategies. Backup and restore is the simplest and cheapest: you back up data to Azure Recovery Services and restore it when needed. Pilot light keeps a minimal version of your environment running in the secondary region, so you only need to scale up during recovery. Warm standby runs a scaled-down but functional version in the secondary region. Active-active runs full production in multiple regions simultaneously.

cards.title: Backup and restore
cards.description: Lowest cost. Restore from backup when needed. RTO can be hours or days depending on data size.

cards.title: Pilot light
cards.description: Core infrastructure always on in secondary region. RTO measured in hours. Good for non-critical workloads.

cards.title: Warm standby
cards.description: Scaled-down but functional environment in secondary region. RTO measured in tens of minutes.

cards.title: Active-active
cards.description: Full production in multiple regions. Lowest RTO, highest cost. Best for mission-critical applications.

data.text: Azure Site Recovery (ASR) replicates virtual machines, physical servers, and on-premises workloads to Azure. It captures changes at the block level and stores them in a storage account. During a failover, ASR spins up VMs in the recovery region from the replicated disks. ASR is especially valuable for legacy applications that cannot be rewritten as cloud-native services.

data.title: ASR replication policy in Bicep
data.content: Create a replication policy that defines how often data is synchronized and how long recovery points are kept.

data.text: Not every workload needs ASR. Azure Backup handles VMs, SQL, Blob, and Kubernetes. Retention policies define how long backups are kept, and soft-delete protects against accidental or malicious deletion. Combine Azure Backup with immutable blob storage for ransomware protection.

terms.definition: Azure-native disaster recovery service for replicating and failing over VMs and physical servers.
A storage and management entity for Azure Backup and ASR.
Blob storage with WORM (write once, read many) policies that prevent backup modification or deletion.

data.title: DR planning checklist
items: Identify critical workloads and assign RTO and RPO targets.
Choose a recovery strategy per workload: backup, pilot light, warm standby, or active-active.
Implement replication using ASR, geo-replication, or Azure Backup.
Document runbooks with exact steps, dependencies, and responsible teams.
Test failover quarterly and after every major architecture change.

data.title: Documentation is part of the plan
data.text: A disaster recovery plan that no one can find or follow during an incident is useless. Store runbooks in a central wiki, run tabletop exercises, and include contact trees with on-call rotations.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Disaster recovery strategies range from cheap and slow to expensive and fast.
Azure Site Recovery is ideal for VM and legacy workloads.
Backup alone is not enough for low-RTO applications.
Regular failover testing is the only way to validate recovery objectives.
data.takeaway: A good DR plan is not just technology—it is technology, runbooks, and practiced execution.
